title: Shin
hook: the letter on the mezuzah, standing for Shaddai

segments.voice: Yesterday, resh, the head of the year. Your line was resh for rosh. Did you catch yourself pausing before you began? Today, a letter you can find on a doorframe. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

A hallway of apartment doors, and on some of them, a small case fixed to the right-hand doorpost, often set at a slant. Wood, metal, glass, clay, sometimes a child's art project. Often there is one letter on the case, raised or painted. Three upright strokes joined at the bottom, like a crown, or a little flame with three tongues. People walk past it every day on the way to work and the grocery store. Some reach up and touch it as they go. Today's letter is that one.
screen: `A SMALL CASE ON THE DOORPOST.` → `THREE STROKES, JOINED AT THE BASE.` → `TOUCHED ON THE WAY OUT.`

segments.voice: Shin. It makes a sh sound, and its shape has three arms rising from one base. The case on the door is a mezuzah, and the word mezuzah means doorpost. Four steps toward the door. First, the command. Inside the case is a small parchment, written by hand, with passages from Deuteronomy, including the Shema. One of its lines gives the case its job. In the King James words: "And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates." The Shema's first word begins with shin. Second, the name. The shin on the outside is usually explained as standing for Shaddai, a name of God. When God appears to Abram in Genesis, the King James words are "I am the Almighty God," and in Hebrew that's El Shaddai. On many mezuzah parchments, the name Shaddai is also written on the back, facing out. Third, a later reading. Some teachers read the letters of Shaddai as initials for a phrase meaning guardian of the doors of Israel. That's a reading added later, not the plain meaning of the name, but it shows what people hoped a door could hold. Fourth, the touch. Some Jews touch the mezuzah on the way in or out, and some kiss their fingers after. It takes less than a second. But it turns a doorway, one of the plainest places in a home, into a moment of remembering. The shin stands right where you cross from private to public and back. The Shema says to keep these words in your heart, and then puts them on the door, where your body passes them whether your heart is ready or not.
screen: `SHIN: THREE ARMS, ONE BASE.` · `WRITE THEM UPON THE POSTS.` · `SHIN FOR SHADDAI.` · `A TOUCH AT THE THRESHOLD.` · then, large: `UPON THE POSTS OF THY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch a doorframe as you pass. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door you go through most often: your front door, your bedroom door, the door at work. See its frame. Imagine your hand resting on it for a second as you pass. Ask what you're carrying through it, out into the day or back home at night. Worry, hurry, a hard conversation, a good mood. Choose one thing you'd like to remember every time you cross. If you pray, you can let the touch be a small prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shin. The three-armed letter on the mezuzah, usually explained as Shaddai, a name of God, on the doorpost of a Jewish home. Today's word.
Your line: shin on the door. Today, touch the doorframe each time you go out and come back in, and remember the one thing you chose. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish homes fix a mezuzah, a case holding a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages, on the right-hand doorpost, often marked with the letter shin for Shaddai; some Jews touch it and kiss their fingers as they pass.

fork.setup: the Shema says to keep these words in your heart. then it says where else to put them. where?
options: on the doorposts of your house, and on your gates.
fork.reveal: on the posts of the house and on the gates. the words go where your body passes them every day.

original.note: Hebrew: Shaddai, a name of God, as in El Shaddai — the name the shin on a mezuzah stands for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a decorative letter on a door.
what it means: shin for Shaddai, on a case holding the Shema, fixed to the doorpost as Deuteronomy commands.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 6:9 and 11:20; Genesis 17:1's El Shaddai; and the later reading of Shaddai as shomer daltot Yisrael.
recall: named for its first two letters

sources.quoted: And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.

notes: Deuteronomy 6:9 and Genesis 17:1 quoted from KJV. Confirm.
Hook's 'right-hand doorposts' and 'often' marked with shin: standard practice described generally. Confirm.
Shaddai written on the back of the parchment given as 'on many mezuzah parchments'. Confirm.
Shomer daltot Yisrael explicitly framed as a later reading, attributed to 'some teachers'. Confirm.
Touching and kissing the mezuzah given as 'some Jews'. Confirm.

Editor: hook no longer opens 'Walk down the hallway...' (a banned walk-into opener) and no longer says the cases are slanted as a rule (slanting is an Ashkenazi custom; 'often set at a slant'); cut the superlative 'the most ordinary place in a home'; varied the four-ways signpost.
